newsitem.title: UK: US stocks in London on standby ahead of Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: US stocks in London on standby ahead of Greenspan.

text.p: U.S. shares were little changed in quiet trade on Wednesday as investors awaited the second phase of Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony, dealers said.

Greenspan, who is scheduled to start the final leg of his semi-annual economic report to the U.S. Congress at 1900 GMT/1400 EST, unsettled markets around the globe last week with aggressive talk about possible interest rate hikes.
"The market is really on hold until we hear what the old chap has to say about rates and stock prices," one market maker said.
A last-minute bout of nerves ahead of the testimony sent U.S. blue chips lower on Tuesday. The Dow Industrials average closed 66.20 points down at 6,852.72.
On Tuesday, Greenspan tried to play down market speculation that his comments about the equities investors' "irrational exuberance" were aimed at affecting the markets.
In an unrelated appearance before the U.S. House of Representative's Budget Committee, the Fed chief said "nobody can affect them in a fundamental way".
"These are very thick, elaborate, international markets which are driven by decisions of millions of people," he said.
Market strategists remained convinced, however, that Greenspan has been been attempting to take the steam out of a sizzling Dow, which has jumped over 75 percent in the past two years alone.
"Greenspan clearly has been trying to talk the market down because he views the current valuation levels as being dangerous," said Trevor Greeton, global strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.

Greeton said Greenspan had been using a tactic of "verbal tightening" in order to condition the market for a hike in the Fed funds rate sometime later this year, hoping investors will discount the tightening when it comes.

"The last thing a central banker wants to see is a stock market crash," Greeton said adding that a recent Merrill Lynch poll of fund managers showed a majority still did not expect a U.S. rate increase this year.

In last month's survey, only around one-third of U.S. based fund managers expected a rate rise in 1997. The Fed funds rate, which currently stands at 6.00 percent, was last raised on 1 February, 1995, from 5.50 percent.
"People are beginning to think that inflation will never rise and Fed funds will never rise," Greeton said.
"Given that backround, Greenspan is clearly worried there will be a sharp knee-jerk market reaction should he raise Fed funds."
U.S. bonds were moderately lower, with the March T-bond down 7/32 to 110-2/32, while the yield on the cash 30-year long bond stood at 6.87 percent by 1035 GMT.
